title: Singapore's PISA socio-economic performance gap and what MOE does about it
asked: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh asked how the Ministry of Education assesses Singapore's ranking of second out of 79 PISA systems on the socio-economic status slope, what specific measures target reducing that slope, and what progress is expected.
response: Ms Jasmin Lau said Singapore's slope between socio-economic status and student performance is steeper than the OECD average and most other systems, because while lower-SES students here outperform their OECD counterparts, higher-SES students outperform by an even larger margin. She said one way to flatten the slope would be to stop higher-performing students doing so well, which she said is not educationally sound, and that MOE uplifts students who need more help without capping those who can excel. Measures she cited include additional support for students from lower-income households or with higher needs, such as school-based after-school programmes. She said MOE will continue to watch the trend as part of a suite of indicators, and wants all Singaporean students to have access to opportunities regardless of SES.

key_points.point: Singapore's association between socio-economic background and performance is steeper than the OECD average and most other systems
key_points.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
key_points.quote: Singapore has a steeper slope representing the association between the socio-economic status (SES) background and performance of our students, compared to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) average and most other systems.

key_points.point: Lower-SES students here do better than OECD peers of similar SES, but higher-SES students outperform by an even larger margin, which produces the steeper slope
key_points.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
key_points.quote: our students from higher-SES homes outperformed their peers by an even larger margin

key_points.point: She said flattening the slope by holding back top performers is not educationally sound
key_points.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
key_points.quote: One simplistic way to flatten the slope is to stop our higher-performing students from doing so well.

key_points.point: MOE's stated approach is to uplift students needing more help without capping those who can excel
key_points.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
key_points.quote: The Ministry of Education (MOE) is committed to uplifting students who need more help, without capping the potential of those who can excel.

key_points.point: Targeted measures include extra support for lower-income and higher-needs students, such as school-based after-school programmes
key_points.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
key_points.quote: providing additional support to students who come from lower-income households or who have higher needs, including school-based after-school programmes for students from more challenging home environments

key_points.point: MOE will keep watching the indicator as part of a wider set of measures of educational outcomes
key_points.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
key_points.quote: Yes, we will continue to watch this trend and this indicator closely, as part of a suite of overall indicators that we use when assessing the overall educational outcomes for our students.

key_points.point: She said the aim is access to opportunities for all students regardless of SES
key_points.speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
key_points.quote: we want to make sure that all Singaporean students have as much access to opportunities as possible, regardless of SES

left_open: What progress is expected, or any timeline, on reducing the slope
Whether MOE would adopt the alternative interpretation of the data that higher-SES students have more opportunities, and how that would change policy
Any assessment of the 2006 Hanushek and Woessmann research on early tracking and educational inequality
supplementary: Whether the SES-performance link reflects unequal access to opportunities, and whether MOE will track the indicator and consider research on early tracking.
